'''3.''' A disease of dogs.

'''blotch''' (bloch), ''v. t.'' [< ''blotch, n.''] To mark with blotches; blot, spot, or blur.

'''blotchy''' (bloch′i), ''a.'' [< ''blotch'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Having blotches; disfigured with blotches: as, “his big, bloated, ''blotchy'' face,” ''Warren.''

'''blote†''', ''a.'' and ''v.'' Obsolete spelling of ''bloat''<sup>1</sup>.

'''blotter''' (blot′ėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' A piece of blotting-paper or other device for absorbing an excess of ink or other fluid, used especially in writing. —'''2.''' In ''com.'', a waste-book in which are recorded all transactions in the order of their occurrence.—'''3.''' The current record of arrests and charges in a police office: called in Great Britain a ''charge-sheet.''

'''blottesque''' (blot-esk′), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ''blot'' + ''-esque.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' In ''painting'', executed with heavy blot-like touches.

'''II.''' ''n.'' A painting executed in this style.

'''blottesquely''' (blot-esk′li), ''adv.'' In a blottesque manner; with blot-like touches: as, to paint ''blottesquely.''

'''blotting-book''' (blot′ing-bu̇k), ''n.'' '''1.''' A book formed of leaves of blotting-paper.—'''2.''' In ''com.'', a blotter. See ''blotter'', 2.

'''blottingly''' (blot′ing-li), ''adv.'' By blotting.

ring.

'''blotty''' (blot′i), ''a.'' [< ''blot''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Full of blots.

'''blouse''' (blouz), ''n.'' [Also less prop. ''blowse''; < F. ''blouse'', of uncertain origin, by some identified with F. dial. ''blaude'', ''biaude'', a smock-frock, < OF. ''bliaut'', ''bliaud'', pl. ''bliaus'', ''bliauz'', an upper garment: see ''bleaunt''. But the connection is phonetically improbable.] '''1.''' A light loose upper garment, made of linen or cotton, worn by men as a protection from dust or in place of a coat. A blue linen blouse is the common dress of French workingmen.
{{smaller block|Lelewel was a regular democrat. He wore a ''blouse'' when he was in Paris, and looked like a workman.
{{right|''H. S. Edwards'', Polish Captivity, I. 270.}}}}
'''2.''' A loosely fitting dress-body worn by women and children.

'''bloused''' (blouzd), ''a.'' [< ''blouse'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Wearing a blouse.
{{smaller block|There was a ''bloused'' and bearded Frenchman or two.
{{right|''Kingsley'', Alton Locke, xxxiii.}}}}

'''blout<sup>1</sup>†''', ''a.'' and ''v.'' Same as ''bloat''<sup>2</sup>.

'''blout<sup>2</sup>†''', ''a.'' [Appar. < D. ''bloot'', bare, naked, with perhaps some confusion as to form with Icel. ''blautr'', soft, wet. Cf. ''blot''<sup>2</sup>, ''blate''<sup>1</sup>, and ''bloat''<sup>1</sup>.] Bare; naked. ''Douglas.'' (''Jamieson.'') [Scotch.]

'''blout'''<sup>3</sup> (blout), ''n.'' [Appar. imitative, after ''blow''<sup>1</sup>, ''blast'', etc.] The sudden breaking of a storm;
readings.c2s2:
a sudden downpour of rain, hail, etc., accompanied by wind. ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]

'''blow'''<sup>1</sup> (blō), ''v.''; pret. ''blew'', pp. ''blown'' (also dial. and colloq. pret. and pp. ''blowed''), ppr. ''blowing''. [= Sc. ''blaw'', < ME. ''blowen'', ''blawen'' (pret. ''blew'', ''blewe'', ''bleu'', ''blwe'', ''blu'', pp. ''blown'', ''blowen'', ''bloun'', ''blawen''), < AS. ''blāwan'' (strong verb, pret. ''bleów'', pp. ''blāwen''), blow, = OHG. ''blāhan'' (strong verb, pp. ''blāhan'', ''blān''), blow, also ''blāen'', ''blājan'', MHG. ''blæwen'', ''blæjen'', G. ''blähen'' (weak verb), blow, puff up, swell, = L. ''flāre'', blow. From the same root, with various formatives, come E. ''blaze''<sup>2</sup>, ''blast'', ''bladder'', perhaps ''blister'', and, from the L., ''flatus'', ''afflatus'', ''flatulent'', ''inflate'', etc.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To produce a current of air, as with the mouth, a bellows, etc.—'''2.''' To constitute or form a current of air, as the wind.
{{smaller block|<poem>A keen north wind that, ''blowing'' dry,
Wrinkled the face of deluge.</poem>{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 842.}}}}
'''3†.''' To make a blowing sound; whistle.—'''4.''' To pant; puff; breathe hard or quickly.
{{smaller block|Here’s Mistress Page at the door, sweating and ''blowing''.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 3.}}}}
'''5.''' To give out sound by being blown, as a horn or trumpet.
{{smaller block|There let the pealing organ ''blow''.
{{right|''Milton'', Il Penseroso, l. 161.}}}}
'''6.''' To spout as a whale.
{{smaller block|A porpoise comes to the surface to ''blow''.
{{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Vert., p. 348.}}}}
'''7.''' To explode, as gunpowder or dynamite; be torn to pieces by an explosion: with ''up'': as, the magazine ''blew up''.—'''8.''' To boast; brag. [Colloq.]

'''3.''' To obliterate so as to render invisible or not distinguishable, as writing or letters with ink: generally with ''out'': as, to ''blot out'' a word or a sentence.
{{smaller block|To ''blot'' old books and alter their contents.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 948.}}}}
Hence—'''4.''' To efface; cause to be unseen or forgotten; destroy; annihilate: followed by ''out'': as, to ''blot out'' a crime, or the remembrance of anything.
{{smaller block|Will not a tiny speck very close to our vision ''blot out'' the glory of the world, and leave only a margin by which we see the blot? ''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, I. 458.
<poem>''Blotting out'' the far-away blue sky,
The hard and close-packed clouds spread silently.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, III. 336.}}}}
'''5.''' To darken or obscure; eclipse. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He sung how earth ''blots'' the moon’s gilded wane.
{{right|''Cowley.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The moon, in all her brother’s beams array’d,
Was ''blotted'' by the earth’s approaching shade.</poem>
{{right|''Rowe'', tr. of Lucan’s Pharsalia, i.}}}}
'''6.''' To dry by means of blotting-paper or the like.
{{smaller block|The ship-chandler clutched the paper, hastily ''blotted'' it, and thrust it into his bosom.
{{right|''G. A. Sala'', The Ship-Chandler.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To obliterate something written.
<poem>E’en copious Dryden wanted or forgot
The last and greatest art, the art to ''blot.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Pope'', Imit. of Horace, II. i. 280.}}}}

'''2.''' To become blotted or stained: as, this paper ''blots'' easily.

'''blot'''<sup>2</sup> (blot), ''n.''   [First at the end of the 16th century; origin unknown. Plausibly referred to Dan. ''blot'' = Sw. ''blott'', bare, exposed; cf. Dan. ''blotte'' = Sw. ''blotta'', lay bare, expose one’s self; Sw. ''blottställa'' = D. ''blootstellen'', expose (the Scand. forms are prob. of LG. origin, < D. ''bloot'', bare, naked, exposed); but there is no historical evidence for the connection.]   In ''backgammon:'' (''a'') A single exposed piece which is liable to be forfeited or taken up. (''b'') The exposure of a piece in this way.—'''To hit the blot''', {{smaller|to take a single exposed piece in the game of backgammon: often used figuratively.}}

{{smaller block|Mr. Ellis ''hits the blot'' when he says that “absolute certainty and a mechanical mode of procedure, such that all men should be capable of employing it, are the two great features of the Baconian system.”
{{right|''The Nation'', April 24, 1884, p. 369.}}}}

'''blotch''' (bloch), ''n.''   [Not found in ME., or in other languages; appar. a var. of ''blot''<sup>1</sup>, affected in sense and form by ''botch''<sup>1</sup>, a pustule, and perhaps by dial. ''blatch'', q. v.]   '''1.''' A pustule upon the skin.

{{smaller block|''Blotches'' and tumours that break out in the body.
{{right|''Spectator'', No. 16.}}}}

'''2.''' A spot of any kind, especially a large irregular spot or blot; hence, anything likened to a mere spot or blot, as a poor painting; a daub.

{{smaller block|Green leaves, frequently marked with dark ''blotches.''
{{right|''Treasury of Botany.''}}}} '''3.''' A disease of dogs.

'''II.''' ''n.'' A painting executed in this style.

{{right|''H. S. Edwards'', Polish Captivity, I. 270.}}}}
'''2.''' A loosely fitting dress-body worn by women and children.

{{smaller block|There was a ''bloused'' and bearded Frenchman or two.
{{right|''Kingsley'', Alton Locke, xxxiii.}}}}

'''blow'''<sup>1</sup> (blō), ''v.''; pret. ''blew'', pp. ''blown'' (also dial. and colloq. pret. and pp. ''blowed''), ppr. ''blowing''.   [= Sc. ''blaw'', < ME. ''blowen'', ''blawen'' (pret. ''blew'', ''blewe'', ''bleu'', ''blwe'', ''blu'', pp. ''blown'', ''blowen'', ''bloun'', ''blawen''), < AS. ''blāwan'' (strong verb, pret. ''bleów'', pp. ''blāwen''), blow, = OHG. ''blāhan'' (strong verb, pp. ''blāhan'', ''blān''), blow, also ''blāen'', ''blājan'', MHG. ''blæwen'', ''blæjen'', G. ''blähen'' (weak verb), blow, puff up, swell, = L. ''flāre'', blow. From the same root, with various formatives, come E. ''blaze''<sup>2</sup>, ''blast'', ''bladder'', perhaps ''blister'', and, from the L., ''flatus'', ''afflatus'', ''flatulent'', ''inflate'', etc.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To produce a current of air, as with the mouth, a bellows, etc.—'''2.''' To constitute or form a current of air, as the wind.
{{smaller block|<poem>A keen north wind that, ''blowing'' dry,
Wrinkled the face of deluge.</poem>{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 842.}}}}
'''3†.''' To make a blowing sound; whistle.—'''4.''' To pant; puff; breathe hard or quickly.
{{smaller block|Here’s Mistress Page at the door, sweating and ''blowing''.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 3.}}}}
'''5.''' To give out sound by being blown, as a horn or trumpet.
{{smaller block|There let the pealing organ ''blow''.
{{right|''Milton'', Il Penseroso, l. 161.}}}}
'''6.''' To spout as a whale.
{{smaller block|A porpoise comes to the surface to ''blow''.
{{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Vert., p. 348.}}}}
'''7.''' To explode, as gunpowder or dynamite; be torn to pieces by an explosion: with ''up'': as, the magazine ''blew up''.—'''8.''' To boast; brag. [Colloq.]

{{smaller block|You ''blow'' behind my back, but dare not say anything to my face. {{right|''Bartlett'', Dict. of Americanisms, p. 48.}}}}
'''9.''' In ''founding'', to throw masses of fluid metal from the mold, as a casting, when, insufficient vent having been provided, the gases and steam are unable to pass off quietly.{{smaller|—'''Blowing off,''' in ''engin.'', the process of ejecting water or sediment from a boiler by means of a current of steam passing through the blow-off pipe.—'''Blowing through,''' in ''engin.'', the act of removing the air from the cylinders, valves, etc., of a steam-engine by a jet of steam previous to setting the engine in motion. Blow-through valves are fitted for this purpose.—'''To blow down,''' to discharge the contents of a steam-boiler.—'''To blow hot and cold,''' to be favorable and then unfavorable; be irresolute.—'''To blow in,''' to start up a blast-furnace, or put it in blast.—'''To blow off,''' to escape with violence and noise: said of steam, gas, etc.—'''To blow out,''' to be out of breath, or blown.—'''To blow over,''' to pass over; pass away after the force is expended; cease, subside, or be dissipated: as, the present disturbances will soon ''blow over''.}}
{{smaller block|A man conscious of acting so infamous a part, would have undertaken no defence, but let the accusations, which could not materially affect him, ''blow over''. {{right|''Goldsmith'', Bolingbroke.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To blow short,''' to be broken-winded: said of a horse.—'''To blow the buck’s horn†.''' See ''buck''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To blow up.''' (''a'') See 7, above. (''b'') To arise, come into existence, or increase in intensity: said of the wind, a storm, etc.}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To throw or drive a current of air upon; fan: as, to ''blow'' the fire. {{smaller block|{{right|''D. G. Rossetti'', A New Year’s Burden.}}}}
'''3.''' To force air into or through, in order—(''a'') To clear of obstructing matter, as the nose. (''b'') To cause to sound, as a wind-instrument.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hath she no husband
That will take pains to ''blow'' a horn before her?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|The bells she jingled and the whistle ''blew.''
{{right|''Pope'', R. of the L., v. 94.}}}}
'''4.''' To form by inflation; inflate; swell by injecting air into: as, to ''blow'' bubbles; to ''blow'' glass.—'''5.''' To empty (an egg) of its contents by blowing air or water into the shell.—'''6.''' To put out of breath by fatigue: as, to ''blow'' a horse by hard riding.
{{smaller block|''Blowing'' himself in his exertions to get to close quarters.
{{right|''T. Hughes.''}}}}
'''7.''' To inflate, as with pride; puff up. [Poetic when ''up'' is omitted.]
{{smaller block|Look, how imagination ''blows'' him.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 4.}}}}
'''8.''' To spread by report, as if “on the wings of the wind.”
{{smaller block|<poem>She’s afraid it will be ''blown'' abroad,
And hurt her marriage. ''B. Jonson'', Alchemist, ii. 1.</poem>
Through the court his courtesy was ''blown.'' ''Dryden.''}}
'''9.''' To drive away, scatter, or shatter by fire-arms or explosives: now always with modifying words (''up'', ''away'', ''to pieces'', etc.): as, to ''blow'' the walls ''up'' or ''to pieces'' with cannon or gunpowder; but formerly sometimes used absolutely.
{{smaller block|<poem>And ’t shall go hard,
But I will delve one yard below their mines,
And ''blow'' them at the moon. ''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 4.</poem>}}

'''10.''' To deposit eggs in; cause to putrefy and swarm with maggots; make fly-blown: said of flies.
{{smaller block|<poem>Rather on Nilus’ mud
Lay me stark naked, and let the water-flies
''Blow'' me into abhorring! {{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., v. 2.}}</poem>}}

'''To blow a coal.''' See ''coal.''—'''To blow one’s own trumpet,''' to sound one’s own praises.—'''To blow out.''' (''a'') To extinguish by a current of air, as a candle. (''b'') To destroy by firearms: as, to ''blow out'' one’s brains; to ''blow'' an enemy’s ship ''out'' of the water.—'''To blow up.''' (''a'') To fill with air; swell: as, to ''blow up'' a bladder or a bubble.
{{smaller block|In summe, he is a bladder ''blown vp'' with wind, which the least flaw crushes to nothing.
{{right|''Bp. Earle'', Micro-cosmographie, A Selfe-conceited Man.}}}}
(''b'') To inflate; puff up: as, to ''blow up'' one with flattery.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Blown up'' with high conceits ingendering pride.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 809.}}</poem>}}
(''c'') To fan or kindle: as, to ''blow up'' a contention.
{{smaller block|<poem>His presence soon ''blows up'' the unkindly fight.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}</poem>}}
(''d'') To burst in pieces by explosion: as, to ''blow up'' a ship by setting fire to the magazine. (''e'') Figuratively, to scatter or bring to naught suddenly: as, to ''blow up'' a scheme. (''f'') To scold; abuse; find fault with. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|<poem>He rails at his cousin, and ''blows up'' his mother.
{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 295.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|Lord Gravelton . . . was ''blowing up'' the waiters in the coffee-room. {{right|''Bulwer'', Pelham, iv.}}}}
(''g'') To raise or produce by blowing.
{{smaller block|<poem>This windy tempest, till it ''blow up'' rain,
Held back his sorrow’s tide, to make it more.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1788.}}</poem>}}

{{smaller|'''To blow upon.''' (''a'') To bring into disfavor or discredit; render stale, unsavory, or worthless.}}
{{smaller block|Since that time, . . . many of the topics, which were first started here, have been hunted down, and many of the thoughts ''blown upon.'' {{right|''Goldsmith'', Essays, Preface.}}}}
{{smaller block|Till the credit of the false witnesses had been ''blown upon.'' {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') To turn informer against: as, to ''blow upon'' an accomplice. [Slang.]}}

'''blow'''<sup>1</sup> (blō), ''n.''   [< ''blow''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''1.''' A blowing; a blast; hence, a gale of wind: as, there came a ''blow'' from the northeast.—'''2.''' The breathing or spouting of a whale.—'''3.''' In ''metal.'': (''a'') The time during which a blast is continued. (''b'') That portion of time occupied by a certain stage of a metallurgical process in which the blast is used. {{smaller|Thus, the operation of converting cast-iron into steel by the Bessemer process is often spoken of as “the blow,” and this first portion is sometimes called the “Bessemer blow” or the blow proper, the second stage being denominated the “boil,” and the third the “fining.”}} '''4.''' An egg deposited by a fly on flesh or other substance; a flyblow.

'''blow'''<sup>2</sup> (blō), ''v.''; pret. ''blew'', pp. ''blown'', ppr. ''blowing''.   [< ME. ''blowen'' (pret. *''blewe'', ''bleou'', pp. ''blown'', ''blowen'', ''blowe''), < AS. ''blōwan'' (pret. ''bleów'', pp. ''geblōwen''), blossom, flower, flourish, = OS. ''blōjan'' = OFries. ''blōia'' = D. ''bloeijen'' = OHG. ''bluojan'', MHG. ''blüejen'', ''blüen'', G. ''blühen'', blow, bloom, = L. ''florere'' (a secondary form),<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
